paper_title: Accelerating Mixture of Block Attention via Dynamic Routing, KV-Centric Execution and Runtime Pipelining

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Mixture of Block Attention (MoBA) reduces long-context computation by selecting key-value (KV) blocks for each query. FlashMoBA implements MoBA efficiently but retains a fixed Top-k budget and query-centric schedule. Fixed Top-k applies one budget across different score distributions and couples routing to task granularity; query-range ownership fragments K/V reuse when several ranges select the same column. We present LightningMoBA, which co-designs selection and execution through dynamic routing, KV-centric ownership, and runtime pipelining. Dynamic routing thresholds MoBA's per-query block scores and directly emits variable-cardinality sparse metadata. KV-centric ownership groups selected rows by (query head, KV block) column, splits high-fanout columns into bounded tasks, and reuses each task's loaded KV tile. On Hopper, pipelining overlaps regular K/V transfers and irregular query gathers with Tensor Core computation. Together, these mechanisms decouple retention from GPU scheduling granularity. At matched Top-16 retention across five checkpoints, LightningMoBA accelerates end-to-end generation by 1.20 to 1.60x while raising mean RULER score from 74.42 to 75.28.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Dense self-attention evaluates all pairwise query-key interactions in sequence, whereas sparse attention reduces this work by routing each query to only subset of keys. On GPUs, however, fewer interactions do not automatically yield proportionally lower latency: score selection, sparse-index construction, irregular data movement, and load imbalance can offset the savings in arithmetic. An efficient sparse attention method must therefore jointly optimize the routing decision and the GPU workload that follows from it. Mixture of Block Attention (MoBA) [1] routes at block granularity: it scores each KV block against the query, retains fixed number of blocks, and computes softmax attention over their tokens. FlashMoBA [2] implements this efficiently, maintaining an ordered Top-k candidate set per query and assigning each CTA logical query range whose selected rows are gathered into dense Tensor Core tiles. Nevertheless, two limitations remain. Fixed Top-k routing assigns the same block budget to queries with different score distributions, retaining weakly related blocks for concentrated scores while discarding relevant blocks for diffuse ones. Maintaining the ordered candidate set also adds routing latency. FlashMoBA organizes metadata by KV block but assigns CTA ownership by logical query range, so several CTAs may claim one (query head, KV block) column and leave cross-CTA reuse to the cache hierarchy. Coupling query-group size to also makes routing parameter determine scheduling granularity. We present LightningMoBA, which preserves MoBAs parameter-free query-block scoring rule and computes standard softmax attention over the retained tokens, but reorganizes routing and execution along three axes  (Fig. 1)  . Our contributions are as follows: 1 LightningMoBA Figure 1. Overview of LightningMoBA. Dynamic threshold routing adapts the retained block count per query and constructs sparse metadata directly; KV-centric execution organizes selected rows by (query head, KV block) column and splits high-fanout columns into bounded work items; runtime pipelining keeps each work units KV tile resident while its query gathers overlap Tensor Core work. Dynamic routing. LightningMoBA replaces the fixed per-query Top-k budget with thresholdbased variable retention rule and emits sparse metadata during score evaluation, without an ordered candidate set or learned auxiliary indexer. KV-centric execution and runtime pipelining. Work is organized by columns indexed by query head and KV block, so each unit reuses its loaded KV tile across the selected rows assigned to it. Fanout-aware partitioning bounds the rows per task, while an asymmetric Hopper pipeline overlaps TMA-based K/V transfers and irregular query gathers with Tensor Core computation. Evaluation and analysis. At matched Top-16 retention across five checkpoints, LightningMoBA accelerates end-to-end generation by 1.20 to 1.60 while increasing mean RULER score from 74.42 to 75.28. Controlled complete-device-path replays on two models reach 2.16 to 2.56 speedup at Top-32, while routing and CSC construction reach 6.99 to 11.25 at Top-64. Same-backend comparisons distinguish execution-backend gains, which dominate at Top-16, from dynamic routings increasing benefit at larger budgets: routing alone yields 1.16 to 1.56 end-to-end speedups at Top-64 on the evaluated two models (Sec. 4.3.2). Training integration using the adapted FlashMoBA backward implementation achieves 1.602 speedup on Qwen3-4B at Top-64 with closely aligned observed training losses (Sec. 4.2.2).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: The efficiency of sparse attention is determined jointly by its selection rule and by the execution path that consumes the resulting sparse pattern.

sections.title: 2.1 Scoring, Granularity, and Budgeting in Sparse Attention
sections.content: Prescribed patterns [3, 4] fix connectivity by design; input-derived patterns [5, 6] cluster or hash tokens, and SSA [7] aligns sparsewith full-attention representations during training. Within content-dependent selection, granularity, scoring, and budget are separate choices: MoBA [1] scores blocks with mean-pooled keys under fixed per-query budget; NSA [8] combines compressed, selected, and sliding-window branches; DSA [9] and MSA [10] use learned indexers, the latter per GQA group; HiLS [11], HySparse [12] and HySparse2 [13] learn summaries or derive routing from preceding full-attention layer. Candidate discovery 2 LightningMoBA is amortized along different axes [1417], and adaptive budgets also appear [18, 19]. Thresholding avoids sorting: FlashPrefill [20] shares one block-level cutoff per query block, while LightningMoBA thresholds MoBAs per-query block scores, so retention differs across individual queries. FlexPrefill [21] adapts each heads sparse pattern to the input context, switching between query-specific and predefined patterns. Its cumulative-attention-based index selection retains querykey indices until target attention mass is reached. In contrast, LightningMoBA preserves MoBAs block scorer and uses per-query block-score thresholds with KV-centric execution. Retrofitting pretrained checkpoints through learned selector is another route [22, 23]. LightningMoBA changes neither weights nor scorer; it replaces only the rule that maps scores to retained set and co-designs the representation and execution of the resulting variable pattern.

sections.title: 2.2 Co-Design of Sparse Attention and Systems
sections.content: The cost of pattern depends on how its interactions are represented and scheduled: FlashMoBA [2] assigns CTA ownership by logical query range; FAST-Prefill [24] co-designs index generation and caching for an FPGA. KV-outer execution is established [1, 10, 25]: fixed Top-k fixes the query-side row degree but leaves the KV-side column degree varying, so reverse indices and splitting popular columns are existing techniques. LightningMoBA extends KV-outer execution to routing graphs with variable query-side degree: under per-query thresholding, both the row degree of each query and the total number of retained pairs are set at run time. It co-designs the routing representation and execution interface, decoupling the per-query budget from the kernels logical task size and dividing high-fanout columns into tasks with bounded query rows.

sections.title: 2.3 High-Performance Kernels on Modern GPUs
sections.content: FlashAttention [26, 27] tiles attention with online softmax; FlashAttention-3 [28] and FlashAttention-4 [29] add warp-specialized producer-consumer pipelines on Hopper and Blackwell. PagedAttention [30] manages KV-cache storage at the serving level, orthogonal to the organization of data movement inside one attention call. These kernels show that tile shape, work ownership, and operand access determine what can overlap. LightningMoBA applies these principles to KV-centric sparse workload with asymmetric operand access: contiguous K/V tiles move through TMA while indexed query rows move through dedicated producer path, both overlapping Tensor Core computation, with tile shapes and warp roles independent of how many blocks each query retains.

sections.content: MoBA assigns the same routing budget to every query, regardless of how its block scores are distributed. sections.title: 3.3 KV-Centric Execution
sections.content: The sparse pattern produced by routing is content-dependent, whether or not its per-query cardinality is fixed. FlashMoBA assigns work by logical query ranges, so queries in different ranges that select the same KV block are handled by different CTAs, causing repeated KV loads and fragmented reuse across query-owned tasks. This limits the useful work each loaded KV tile can amortize. We instead organize the sparse pattern by (query head, KV block) columns and assign execution around these columns (Sec. 2.2). Queries selecting the same block under query head are therefore grouped under the same KV-owned column, allowing each work unit to reuse its loaded KV tile across its assigned rows. Because columns task size is proportional to its fanout, assigning an entire column to one CTA can leave long-running tail. We therefore separate two decisions: ownership, which determines which KV column task belongs to, and task size, which partitions high-fanout columns into bounded work units. sections.title: 3.4 Runtime Pipelining
sections.content: KV-centric execution creates asymmetric operand access: K/V tiles remain contiguous, whereas rows must be gathered from the routing metadata. We assign regular K/V transfers to the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) and irregular gathers to producer path, allowing both paths to be staged concurrently with Tensor 7 Core computation. The implementation targets Hoppers TMA, WGMMA and warp-specialized execution model; Sec. B.3 discusses portability. LightningMoBA

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate end-to-end inference and training performance, controlled execution and routing costs, and long-context quality. Inference comparisons are training-free; training integration is evaluated separately under the settings in Sec. 4.2.2. Model configurations, benchmark settings, and timing scopes are specified below and in the corresponding result sections. Models The evaluation uses five checkpoints: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (Qwen3-4B), Qwen3-235B-A22B, Qwen3-32B-YaRN4, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Llama-3.1-8B), and GQA-30B-A3B, an internal GQA model (30B total, 3B active) whose architecture follows Qwen3 and is trained from scratch. These span dense and mixture-of-experts architectures as well as different GQA grouping ratios; checkpoint sources are listed with the full setup in Appendix D. Each reported configuration identifies the checkpoint revision, tested context lengths, head configuration, and the layers to which sparse attention is applied. We compare against an optimized implementation of the same block-attention method; its baseline definition, training-free protocol and model sources are in Appendix D.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: LightningMoBA keeps MoBAs scoring function and retained-token softmax while decoupling retention from task formation: threshold routing adapts retention to each score distribution, KV-centric ownership and fanout-aware splitting form reusable bounded tasks, and Hopper pipelining overlaps K/V movement, query gathering and Tensor Core work. At matched Top-16 retention these mechanisms accelerate end-to-end 15 LightningMoBA generation by 1.20 to 1.60 across five checkpoints while increasing mean RULER score from 74.42 to 75.28; in controlled replays, complete device-path speedup grows to 2.16 to 2.56 at Top-32, while routing and CSC construction reach 6.99 to 11.25 at Top-64. Same-backend comparisons show that execution optimizations account for most Top-16 acceleration, while dynamic routing provides increasing benefits at larger budgets, reaching 1.16 to 1.56 end-to-end speedups at Top-64 on the evaluated two models. End-to-end Qwen3-4B training with the adapted FlashMoBA backward implementation achieves 1.602 speedup at Top-64, with closely aligned cross-entropy losses over the evaluated 100-step run. These results support the applicability of the design to both inference and training, while distinguishing execution-backend improvements from routing-policy gains.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: The study is algorithmic and systems-level: it changes the selection rule, task formation and data movement of block-sparse attention and reports measurements on public benchmarks. No human subjects, human annotations, or personally identifiable or sensitive data are involved, and the study does not target high-risk application domain. We foresee no immediate ethical concerns arising from this line of systems work.

sections.title: Reproducibility Statement
sections.content: The threshold rule, ownership model, task decomposition and pipeline schedule are specified in Section 3, with the streaming metadata construction and the forward-pass pseudocode deferred to Appendix and Algorithm 1. Section 4.1 lists the checkpoints, context lengths and benchmark. End-to-end inference and training are reported in Sections 4.2.1 and 4.2.2, respectively; external sparse baselines are reported in Appendix C.3. System ablations and the complete attention path breakdown appear in Sec. 4.3. Long-context quality is analyzed in Sec. 4.4. The appendix retains detailed protocols, profiler counters, rank-imbalance analyses, and full per-task results. Proofs of both lemmas appear in Appendix G. Four of the five checkpoints are publicly released; GQA-30B-A3B is an internal model that cannot be distributed. The code repository is https://github.com/Tencent/LightningMoBA.

sections.content: A.1 Complexity Analysis call has four stages, and under the reference design of Sec. 3.1 they scale as O(N2d/B) (scoring), O(N2k/B) (selection), O(Z) (index), O(ZBd) (attention), (10) where scoring and selection remain dense over the candidate blocks, while the emitted metadata volume and the attention work scale with the realized pattern. The candidate-set update within each query is comparison-bound and involves sequential dependence, with cost increasing in both and k, since the reference router maintains an ordered candidate set. The three design axes act on different terms of Eq. (10); beyond arithmetic work, the proposed execution also changes memory-traffic multiplicity and scheduling granularity. Table 11 summarizes each component against its corresponding reference design, which differs by component. Table 11. Arithmetic, movement, and scheduling costs for one attention call. Each row states its own reference design, and data-dependent quantities appear as realized rather than bounded. Component Reference design Proposed design Scoring Selection Index construction Attention arithmetic O(ZBd) one pass, O(N2d/B) ordered k-set, O(N2k/B) count + prefix-sum + scatter, O(Z) K/V movement Longest work item O(Λ(M) CBd) maxh,j wh,j two passes, same asymptotic order threshold test, O(N2/B) scan + emit, O(Nn + Z) unchanged, O(ZBd) O(Λ CBd) T/mMMA Threshold selection removes that k-dependent ordered-set maintenance, so the improvement is against the procedure Eq. (10) prices rather than against Top-k in general, while requiring two score passes to obtain the per-query maximum before any comparison. Neither pass materializes floating-point score matrix. Index construction additionally scans the packed candidate mask, giving O(Nn + Z) work at candidate granularity. Because threshold routing does not impose fixed per-query retention budget, is data-dependent and can reach Θ(N2/B) in the dense-block limit, so attention complexity must be compared at matched realized sparsity; Sec. 4.3.2 provides this controlled comparison. KV-centric ownership and fanout splitting leave the O(ZBd) arithmetic unchanged; they instead reduce fetch multiplicity and bound the longest serial work item, trading reuse against parallelism. Every bound here is per attention call and does not by itself determine end-to-end latency, which Sec. 4 measures.

sections.content: B.1 Replay Protocols and Supplementary Diagnostics Unless otherwise stated, we replay captured BF16 tensors from Qwen3-4B and GQA-30B-A3B at 32K and 128K on single rank, retaining the complete 32-query-head/8-KV-head shape with head dimension 128 and block size 128. Comparisons use identical causal and compulsory-block rules. Latencies are medians of 50 measurements after 10 warmups; each subsection specifies its timing scope and CUDA Graph usage. These device replays exclude host-side work and model inference, and remove the cross-rank synchronization present in the TP8 main experiments. Execution-only comparisons hold routing metadata fixed; routingpolicy comparisons match the realized number of selected query-block pairs. The following protocols supplement the cumulative and single-component results in Sec. 4.3; optional-only fanout diagnostics remain here. 19 LightningMoBA B.1.1 Cumulative Implementation Ablation Protocol Table 3 adds KV-centric ownership, fanout splitting, query-gather pipelining, and threshold routing to FlashMoBA. At each Top-k budget, the first four variants consume one identical saved CSC pattern. Their timed replays execute the Top-k router but feed the saved pattern to downstream kernels, controlling run-torun changes in column counts. The threshold variant uses separate saved pattern with valid pair count matched within 0.05%; selected pair identities may differ. Timing includes pooling, routing, required reverse-index construction, device-side worklist construction, attention, and merge. We use eager CUDA events because the baselines segmented-sort path is not graphcapturable in this replay. These fixed-pattern device-path costs are distinct from live router-to-attention invocations and the CUDA Graph kernel timings below. Adjacent columns are implementation steps rather than single-switch causal tests: +Split replaces the specialized unsplit kernel with worklist kernel, and +Pipeline also changes the kernel family and merge path. Secs. 4.3.4 and 4.3.5 isolate these effects within fixed kernels. Sampled-row output validation compares the same-pattern Top-k variants against FlashMoBA; it excludes the threshold arm, which selects different pairs. Results are discussed in Sec. 4.3.1. B.1.2 Routing Cost Across Budgets Protocol We compare the cost of producing attention-ready CSC metadata. FlashMoBA scores candidates once while maintaining an ordered k-element set; threshold routing scores them twice, first for the per-query maximum and then for threshold selection and packed-mask updates. This tests the extra score pass against ordered-set maintenance. We replay captured and mean-pooled at 16K, 32K, 64K, and 128K for {16, 32, 64}. separate α is calibrated outside timing for each model, length, and k, matching total attention-visible valid CSC pairs within 0.05% across all 24 comparisons. Compulsory blocks count toward this total and occupy slots within FlashMoBAs fixed budget. Threshold CSC columns use device-resident counts to delimit their valid prefixes. CUDA Graph timings include scoring, selection, and CSC construction, excluding mean pooling and attention. Results appear in Sec. 4.3.2 and Table 4. separate 128K decision-stage measurement excludes final CSC offset/scatter construction but retains scoring, selection, and output/count updates. B.1.3 Ownership Ablation Protocol We compare query-centric and KV-centric execution using identical Q/K/V and Top-16 CSC metadata, with one sink block and two-block local window. The captures contain post-normalization, post-RoPE Q/K and corresponding V. Qwen3-4B is captured with one tensor-parallel rank; GQA-30B-A3Bs eight rank captures are concatenated along the head dimension for the full-head replay. The KV-centric variant assigns one CTA per (h, j) column, using an unsplit 64 64 kernel and onlinesoftmax merge, with fanout splitting, query splitting, and worklist scheduling disabled. Timing covers the query-centric attention kernel or the KV-centric kernel plus its required merge; routing and reverse-index construction are excluded from both. Here we retain supplementary profiler counters and tensor-parallel rank-imbalance measurements. B.2.1 Pipeline Stall and Activity Analysis We profile the attention kernel of the serial and pipelined variants from Sec. 4.3.5 on the two 128K captures using Nsight Compute. These profiler runs do not supply the CUDA Graph timings. With pipelining, long-scoreboard stall falls from about 63% to below 8%, while tensor-pipe activity rises from about 7% to 17% and SM issue activity from about 15% to 36%  (Table 12)  . KV-centric ownership, fanout-aware splitting, and reverse-index metadata determine how routed work is represented and scheduled, independent of TMA or WGMMA. Our Hopper implementation maps the regular K/V path to TMA, the irregular query-gather path to dedicated producer warp, and matrix computation to WGMMA, allowing data movement and Tensor Core computation to overlap. Porting to another accelerator therefore requires hardware support, or an alternative software mechanism, for concurrent contiguous transfers, indexed gathers, and matrix operations, but does not require changing the routing rule or ownership abstraction. Consequently, the pipelining gains reported here are tied to Hopper, whereas the routing and ownership analyses are hardware-independent. B.3.2 Impact on Tensor-Parallel Load Balance Fanout-aware splitting bounds the work assigned to one KV column within rank, but it does not redistribute work between tensor-parallel ranks. We analyze an instrumented Qwen3-4B RULER-128K prefill profile with eight ranks, each owning four query heads and one KV head. Excluding the first request, 12 requests and 36 layers provide 432 complete request-layer groups. For each group, we divide the maximum rank-local value by the mean across ranks; Table 13 aggregates these ratios. The observed rank-level timing is consistent with workload imbalance: the rank with the most selected query-block pairs is also the slowest K1 rank in 428 of 432 request-layer groups. Table 13. Rankaware budget control or cross-rank work redistribution could reduce the slow-rank path, but the former can alter the selected pattern and the latter incurs communication. sections.title: D Additional Setup Details
sections.content: Baselines The primary sparse baseline is MoBAs fixed Top-k routing [1] executed by the FlashMoBA kernel [2], not an unoptimized reference implementation. This compares LightningMoBA against an optimized implementation of the same underlying block-attention method. The original-attention quality reference uses each checkpoints native attention configuration; for hybrid models, this retains the prescribed slidingwindow layers. It is reference score, not an assumed upper bound on every task. Results identify the kernel behind each attention variant. The effect of each design component is examined through the cumulative ablation in Sec. 4.3.1  (Table 3)  , rather than inferred solely from shared implementation codebase. Training-free protocol For each checkpoint, model weights are held fixed across the attention variants. Neither sparse method requires additional model fine-tuning or an auxiliary learned indexer for the comparison. LightningMoBA retains MoBAs block-scoring function and changes the block-selection rule and its execution. Training-free therefore describes the inference-time adaptation, not the training history of the checkpoint or equality of the resulting model outputs. Threshold calibration For each model and target Top-k budget, we calibrate α on held-out sample that is disjoint from the test evaluation. We sweep α and select the value whose mean realized number of retained blocks most closely matches the corresponding Top-k budget. We then verify the matched budget on separate validation sample and fix α before running the reported evaluation. No task labels or benchmark scores are used during calibration. Model sources Qwen3-4B1, Qwen3-235B-A22B2, Qwen3-32B-YaRN43, Llama-3.1-8B4, and GQA-30B-A3B, an internal model with no external release. Metrics and measurement protocol We report two timing quantities and keep them separate. End-to-end results use generation-loop wall time over complete evaluation run, system-level measurement in which both variants execute the same dense decode path. Controlled replays instead time the complete attention path, including routing, sparse-index construction and attention computation, with component timings where available. The two are not combined into single speedup claim, and prefill, decode and full-model inference measurements are distinguished rather than merged. Quality comparisons report task scores alongside the original-attention reference and their differences. The run specification records hardware, parallelism, precision, software and kernel versions, batch and sequence lengths, warmup and timing repetitions, the aggregation statistic, and CUDA Graph usage. Common hardware, input, precision and timing conditions are held fixed within each comparison; method-specific kernel implementations and versions are recorded separately. Throughput, memory use and kernel-utilization measurements can provide additional diagnostics where collected, but are not substitutes for the stated latency and quality comparisons. Main experiments use tensor parallelism of eight unless noted, and ablations replay on one rank. Comparison protocol The primary comparison targets matched average retained-block budgets, with threshold parameters calibrated and validated on held-out samples before evaluation. Where full-evaluation retention measurements are available, we report realized deviations explicitly (Appendix C.2.1, Table 16). Both sparse methods use the same block size and causal-boundary convention; compulsory blocks count toward the budget. We compare latency and quality without assuming that the selected blocks are identical. We use the two-pass streaming construction of the routing stage in Fig. 1: the first pass computes the per-query maximum over complete blocks preceding the querys own block, and the second recomputes optional-block scores against the equivalent cutoff . Compulsory blocks are retained directly, emitting candidate bitmask with per-query and per-column retained counts. At one bit per candidate block the bitmask occupies O(Nn/32) machine words regardless of realized retention, and each candidate needs only scalar comparison and bit update, unlike an ordered Top-k candidate set per query. The execution in Sec. 3.3 consumes the transpose of these decisions: for each KV block, the query rows that selected it. Since the per-column counts are already available, an exclusive prefix sum determines each columns contiguous range, after which scatter pass writes the retained query indices into compact buffer. E.4 Pipeline Overlap and Latency Hiding Gathering queries is the irregular half of the loop; assigning these gathers to the compute warps interleaves indexed-load stalls with matrix instruction issue. We therefore use one 128-thread consumer warpgroup and one 32-thread producer warp. The producer decodes the next query tiles routing metadata, including the selected query-row indices and, for each row, the extent of its causal mask within the block, and then issues the gathers, while the consumer executes QK, the softmax, and PV. Queries flow through two-stage ring buffer  (Fig. 8)  , so stage + 1 is gathered while stage is consumed, and index processing overlaps matrix work instead of preceding it. Once QK and the softmax have consumed staged tile we release the stage before PV and the epilogue. K/V residency removes the regular transfers from the steady-state loop, and early release shortens stages shared-memory lifetime, letting the producer refill that stage sooner. Sec. 4.3.5 compares serial and overlapped query gathering within the same SM90 kernel and reports the resulting latency changes.
